Definition: Whether digital payment systems and access points (apps, USSD, agents) are designed to accommodate persons with disabilities (visual, hearing, mobility, cognitive impairments), and disability-disaggregated coverage rates if data available.
Comments: No credible, Nigeria-specific evidence was found in the sources reviewed that documents mandatory accessibility/disability-access requirements or audited accessibility compliance for national digital payment channels (searched: CBN payments policy pages, NIBSS pages, SIIPS case study).

revision_notes: Fast-path search (Step 0) surfaced multiple 2024-2026 sources (Punch, allAfrica, DPI Africa, Ripples Nigeria) documenting Nigeria's Discrimination Against Persons with Disabilities (Prohibition) Act 2018 and CBN ATM operational guidelines (requiring at least 2% of ATMs to carry tactile graphic symbols within five years, with sanctions for non-compliance), alongside extensive, corroborated reporting that in practice most banking apps, USSD channels and ATMs remain inaccessible to blind, low-vision and mobility-impaired customers. revised_comments: Nigeria's Discrimination Against Persons with Disabilities (Prohibition) Act 2018 requires public services, including banks, to be accessible, and the Central Bank of Nigeria's ATM operational guidelines mandate that at least 2% of deployed ATMs carry tactile graphic symbols for visually impaired customers within five years of release, with sanctions available for non-compliance. In practice, however, independent surveys of Nigerian banks by disability advocacy groups (the Association for the Blind in Nigeria and the Centre for Infrastructural and Technological Advancement for the Blind) find that most mobile banking apps, USSD channels and ATMs remain largely unusable for blind and low-vision customers, citing screen-reader incompatibility, unlabelled buttons, timed USSD menus and facial-recognition verification steps as recurring barriers; some blind customers are required to sign indemnity forms to obtain ATM cards. A small number of individual bank initiatives exist, such as UBA's braille account-opening form and First Bank's plans for voice-assisted ATMs, and the Central Bank of Nigeria and the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission are engaging disability groups and the National Commission for Persons with Disabilities to improve compliance. Overall, accessible design remains partial and inconsistently implemented rather than the norm.

Definition: Whether refugees, asylum seekers, internally displaced persons, migrants, and stateless persons can legally access and open digital payment accounts, and practical barriers or enablers for these populations.
Comments: No credible, Nigeria-specific evidence was found in the sources reviewed that documents targeted access provisions for refugees/migrants to use the national digital payment system (searched: CBN payments policy pages, NIBSS pages, SIIPS case study, NDPC/NDPA materials).
redteam_note: Scored 0/Unknown with no source — confirm it is truly unknown, not just unresearched. No data year recorded — provenance/recency unknown.
revision_notes: Fast-path search (Step 0) surfaced the Central Bank of Nigeria's own Customer Due Diligence Regulations 2023 (Regulation 32, cbn.gov.ng), a 2021 CBN circular (reported by ThisDayLive, Businessday and others) instructing banks to accept the Machine Readable Convention Travel Document and National Commission for Refugees/Migrants/IDPs Refugee ID Card, and a UNHCR ReliefWeb update documenting over 9,000 refugee bank accounts and 1,500 ATM cards issued via Standard Chartered and First Bank of Nigeria. Per Step 0.2, moved from fast path to full path because authoritative primary sources (CBN regulation text itself) exist and were fetched/read. Recalculated from 0 (Unknown) to 3 (Yes): refugee ID is a CBN-mandated acceptable KYC document for account opening, and access is demonstrated in practice, not merely on paper.
revised_comments: Refugees, asylum seekers and other forcibly displaced persons in Nigeria have a legally recognised route to open bank and payment accounts. The Central Bank of Nigeria's Customer Due Diligence Regulations 2023 (Regulation 32) direct financial institutions to accept identification issued by the Nigeria Immigration Service or other recognised government agency when rendering banking services to refugees and asylum seekers, formalising an earlier 2021 CBN circular that instructed banks to accept the Machine Readable Convention Travel Document and the Refugee Identity Card issued by the National Commission for Refugees, Migrants and Internally Displaced Persons as valid means of identification. In practice, this framework has supported UNHCR-facilitated account opening for displaced populations, including over 9,000 bank accounts opened for Cameroonian refugees in partnership with Standard Chartered and First Bank of Nigeria, with the first 1,500 ATM cards issued in 2021, and Nigeria's Bank Verification Number biometric system is cited internationally as a model for e-KYC-enabled financial inclusion of forcibly displaced persons. Access is both regulator-mandated and evidenced in practice, though it typically depends on partner-facilitated onboarding (e.g. UNHCR, banks) rather than unassisted walk-in account opening.
